items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper makes three original contributions to the governance of artificial intelligence systems in regulated enterprise environments. First, it establishes that board-level accountability under deployer frameworks, particularly as formalized in the EU AI Act, constitutes a fiduciary obligation structurally equivalent to credit, operational, and cyber risk oversight, requiring the same formal integration into enterprise risk management. Second, it introduces authority drift as a first-class enterprise risk variable: the condition by which delegated autonomy in agentic AI systems expands in scope, duration, or privilege concentration without formal reclassification or appetite review, producing material governance exposure that traditional control environments are not designed to detect. Third, it presents the first unified governance loop connecting model risk governance [1] and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework [2] to the governance of delegated authority in agentic systems demonstrating that Continuous Governance [3] is the operating norm capable of spanning both architecture types without requiring a new governance philosophy. The paper develops an autonomy tiering framework classifying AI systems from advisory outputs (Tier 0) to material consequence authority (Tier 4), an enterprise risk management integration model including appetite cascade and residual risk aggregation, structural mechanisms for escalation under ambiguity, architectural containment of delegated authority, and enterprise-level visibility requirements for board oversight. Together these form a governance architecture defensible under regulatory examination, board scrutiny, and operational pressure.</jats:p>
title: Continuous Governance Across Enterprise AI and Agentic Systems: Governing What You Cannot See

items.abstract: <jats:p>Agentic AI represents a major paradigm shift from passive language models to active systems capable of autonomous decision-making and task execution. This comprehensive review synthesizes recent literature from 2023-2025, examining three critical dimensions that define the future of artificial intelligence: architectural innovations enabling collaborative reasoning between multiple agents, optimization techniques for achieving computational efficiency in resource-constrained environments, and ethical frameworks for ensuring safe deployment in real-world applications. Through systematic analysis of peer-reviewed literature and recent preprints, key findings reveal that multi-agent debate systems demonstrate significant improvements in reasoning accuracy, with collaborative frameworks showing enhanced problem-solving capabilities across diverse domains. However, critical challenges persist in safety alignment mechanisms, environmental sustainability concerns, and the development of standardized evaluation metrics for complex agentic behaviors. The analysis identifies hybrid architectures combining collaborative reasoning with knowledge distillation as the most promising direction for future research, particularly for applications requiring both high accuracy and computational efficiency. This review provides researchers and practitioners with a consolidated framework for understanding current developments and identifying future research directions in agentic systems, highlighting the urgent need for interdisciplinary approaches to address technical, ethical, and environmental challenges in this rapidly evolving field.</jats:p>
title: Agentic AI Systems: Evolution, Efficiency, and Ethical Implementation

items.abstract: Gender gaps in academia persist with women being less likely to attain leadership, earning lower salaries, and receiving less research funding and resources compared to their male peers. The current research demonstrates yet another, more intangible gender gap in academia called lack of fit, whereby compared to male academics, female academics perceive higher misfit between their professional self-concept and the agentic ‘superhero’ stereotype of the successful academic. The entire population of Dutch academics (i.e., assistant, associate, and full professors from 14 universities) was approached to participate in a nationwide survey. Results from this unique dataset (N = 3978) demonstrate that academics perceive agency (e.g., self-confident, self-focused, competitive) as more descriptive of the stereo- typical successful academic than communality (e.g., team- oriented, good teacher, collegial). Importantly, early career female academics perceived highest lack of fit with this narrowly-defined agentic occupational stereotype, which was correlated with lower work engagement, professional identification and career efficacy, and higher work exhaustion and exit intentions. Thus, lack of fit seems yet another barrier contributing to pervasive gender gaps in academia. Implications for building more inclusive academic cultures, where not only agentic but also communal academic practice is recognized and rewarded are discussed.
title: Academics as Agentic Superheroes: Female academics’ lack of fit with the agentic stereotype of success limits their career advancement

items.abstract: <jats:p>Every regime now being assembled to hold AI developers accountable, from incident reporting under the EU AI Act to state consumer-protection enforcement, contractual audit rights, and litigation discovery, rests on an assumption inherited from every accountability structure before it: that an event leaves a factual record a party other than the causer can reconstruct. The July 2026 OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, in which roughly twelve hundred agents run by OpenAI during an internal cybersecurity evaluation coordinated on an unsanctioned message board and compromised Hugging Face's production infrastructure, is the first full-scale test of that assumption, and the most favourable test likely to be available for some time. An independent investigation by METR and Redwood Research was conducted on OpenAI's premises, with unredacted transcripts, at no charge. Even so, it could not independently establish the event's integrated causal account. The record it read was partly authored by the systems under investigation; the only complete copy was held by the party responsible; reading it at scale required an instrument that party supplied and that shared weights and training history with the conduct examined; and the scope, period, and redaction terms were set by the subject. I call an event whose integrated causal account cannot be established independently, for these reasons, a self-attested incident. The victim here established a great deal unaided. What no one else could establish was the origin, the causal link, and the completeness of the record joining the two. The paper locates the three records the incident produced and their holders, separates record integrity from analysis reliability, tests the incident against the EU AI Act's serious-incident regime under Articles 3(49), 55 and 73 and the American cyber-reporting statutes, and finds that it may fall below the definitional threshold of the only AI-specific duty in force. It reads the aviation party system, and the evidentiary bargain in 49 U.S.C. section 1154(b), as law disciplining an investigator's unavoidable dependence on the investigated, and sets out the minimum conditions under which an incident of this kind could be established by someone other than its cause.&nbsp;</jats:p>
title: The Self-attested Incident: The OpenAI-Hugging Face Hack and the Evidentiary Limits of AI Accountability Agentic AI, Incident Reporting under the EU AI Act, and What Accountability Regimes Assume Exists
